rows.meaning: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)
The Unit section answers the first question that any money raises, namely what the money is called and in what pieces it is counted
The unit of currency is bitcoin with a small b, abbreviated BTC; the system is Bitcoin with a capital B.
The satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be recorded, one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin; amounts are counted in whole satoshis.
The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows
New bitcoin is created on a schedule that halves the subsidy every 210000 blocks, so the total supply stays just below 21 million.
The block subsidy halves every 210000 blocks; at block 840000, on 2024-04-20, it fell to 3.125 bitcoin.
The block subsidy is the amount of new bitcoin that a block may create for its miner; it starts at 50 bitcoin and halves every 210000 blocks.
The Price section addresses a question that every newcomer asks, namely who sets the price of bitcoin
The price of bitcoin is set by markets: a floating exchange rate that moves with supply and demand.
A volume-weighted average prices a currency pair by weighting each trade's price by its volume, so larger trades count for more.
The Issuance section is about who creates money and by what rule
A central bank is the institution that controls the creation of a national currency; Bitcoin has none, and its issuance is set by rules.
A clearing house is a central party that records and settles transactions; traditional digital money relied on one, and the term clearing means the confirmation of a payment.
Mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank.
Because issuance diminishes and ends, the currency is deflationary over the long term; the last non-zero subsidy falls in the year 2140 at the target pace.
The Network branch is about the community of computers that runs Bitcoin and the way it agrees on a single history without a leader
Consensus is the state in which the participants of the network agree on the same record of transactions
Proof of work makes adding a block costly and easy to check; a toy version searches for a number whose SHA-256 hash starts with zeros.
The double-spend problem is the possibility of spending one unit of digital money twice; Bitcoin's consensus prevents it without a central clearinghouse.
Mining is the repeated computation, referring to a list of recent transactions, by which a participant tries to add a block and earn the reward.
The difficulty of the work is adjusted every 2016 blocks so that, on average, one block is found every 10 minutes whatever the total computing power.
The Byzantine Generals' Problem asks how participants without a leader can agree on a course of action over an unreliable network; Bitcoin's proof of work is a practical solution.
The History section tells where Bitcoin came from
The 2008 paper by Satoshi Nakamoto that first described Bitcoin as a purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash.
The software that Nakamoto published in 2009 and many programmers have revised since; Bitcoin Core is its descendant and includes a wallet.
Satoshi Nakamoto is the alias of the person or people who designed Bitcoin; their identity is unknown and they withdrew from the public in April 2011.
Hashcash is a proof-of-work scheme proposed by Adam Back in 1997 to throttle abuse of un-metered resources such as email; Bitcoin's proof of work descends from it.
Digital currencies before Bitcoin used cryptography but were centralized and therefore easy to attack, which is the problem Bitcoin was designed to avoid.

The Standards section collects the two social mechanisms through which Bitcoin is documented and developed: the numbered improvement proposals through which changes are discussed, and the open source licence under which the software is shared
A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) is a numbered design document that specifies a change or a convention; BIP 39 describes the mnemonic code behind recovery codes.
Open source software is distributed with its source code under terms that allow free redistribution, modification and derived works.
The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is an international organization that develops web standards; its finished standards are called Recommendations.
A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin
The platform of a wallet is the kind of device and software environment on which it runs
The first type of Bitcoin wallet, run on a general-purpose operating system such as Windows or macOS.
The most common type of Bitcoin wallet, run on a smartphone operating system such as iOS or Android.
A wallet used through a web browser, whose data usually lives on a server owned by a third party.
A hardware signing device stores keys and signs transactions with special-purpose hardware; it must be paired with a full-featured wallet to send and receive.
The node type of a wallet describes how much of the network's work the wallet does for itself
A program that validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions itself and may serve data to other programs.
A client that keeps the wallet locally but relies on a full node or server for most data and validates only partly.
A third-party API client uses a remote system's programming interface instead of the Bitcoin network and trusts it for correct information and privacy.
In the peer-to-peer network, full nodes are the peers and lightweight wallets are clients that depend on one or more peers for valid data.
Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds
A wallet where only the user holds the keys, so only the user controls and can lose the bitcoin.
A custodial wallet or account is one where a third party, the custodian, holds the keys and manages the funds for the user.
The Backup section is about getting a wallet back after something goes wrong
A recovery code of words, numbers or letters chosen at random by the wallet, from which all its keys are generated and from which the wallet can be restored.
Wallet metadata is the data a user adds to a wallet, such as labels on addresses and transactions; a recovery code does not restore it.
The Usage branch follows the chapter's story of Alice and Joe: how Alice receives her first address, how she acquires her first bitcoin, and how Joe sends it
The Address section explains the destination of a payment
A number derived from the private key that others use to pay you; it is registered nowhere, and a new one per invoice protects privacy.
An invoice is a payment request that a wallet can read, carrying a destination address and often an amount and a description.
Using the same address for several payments lets others link and total them; a new address for each payment protects privacy.
Privacy in Bitcoin is pseudonymous: payments are public and attached to addresses, not names, until an address is linked to an identity.
The Transfer section explains what happens when Joe sends bitcoin to Alice
Receiving shows an address or invoice; sending signs a transaction that spends to someone else's address.
A transaction is a signed data structure that expresses a transfer of value; it is broadcast over the network, collected into a block, and made permanent on the blockchain.
A transaction's inputs identify the funds it spends and its outputs assign amounts to new owners; any difference between the totals is the fee.
A transaction fee is the amount a sender adds for the miner who includes the transaction in a block; a higher fee gives faster confirmation.
A confirmation counts the blocks that contain a transaction or follow it; each one makes reversal less likely, and the inclusion in a block is the clearing of the payment.
Bitcoin transactions are irreversible, unlike card payments, bank transfers and other electronic payments, which can be reversed.
An offchain payment moves value without recording every payment in the public blockchain, which lowers cost and improves privacy but changes what a backup must cover.
A payment channel is a class of techniques that lets users make many Bitcoin transactions without committing all of them to the blockchain; typically only two transactions are recorded.
The Lightning Network connects payment channels so that a payment can be routed through several of them, and any peer can pay any other even without a direct channel.
An electronic payment is a payment made over an electronic network; credit cards, debit cards, PayPal and bank transfers are reversible, unlike Bitcoin transactions.
The semantic bridge connects the chapter's central idea with the theme of this course, semantic technologies
A W3C Decentralized Identifier is an identifier that its controller can prove control over without a central registry, applying the principle of control by keys to identity.
A verifiable credential expresses claims made by an issuer, such as a driver's licence or education certificate, in a form protected by digital signatures that a holder can present to a verifier.
The Acquisition section lists the ways in which a newcomer obtains a first bitcoin, which is the practical problem a reader faces as soon as the wallet is installed
The least complicated way to get a first bitcoin: buy directly from someone who has some.
Earning bitcoin means selling a product or service and being paid in it.
A Bitcoin ATM is a machine that accepts cash and sends bitcoin to a smartphone wallet.
A currency exchange is a market where buyers and sellers swap bitcoin and local currency, usually through a linked bank account.
Identity verification is the check of a customer's identity and credit-worthiness that companies converting traditional payments into bitcoin usually require.
The Foundations branch collects the general technical ideas that the rest of the chapter takes for granted
Cryptography is the science of transforming data so that its meaning is hidden, so that undetected alteration is prevented, or so that unauthorised use is prevented
A hash function maps data of any length to a fixed-length fingerprint; SHA-256 produces 256 bits, and any change to the input gives a different result.
A digital signature is a value computed from data and a private key that anyone holding the matching public key can use to verify the origin and integrity of the data.
Public-key cryptography uses a pair of mathematically related keys, one public and one private, so that what one key does only the other can undo.
A private key is the secret half of a key pair; in Bitcoin it is a very large number whose holder alone can sign transactions that spend the corresponding bitcoin.
Entropy is a measure of unpredictability, counted in bits; a wallet needs enough of it that nobody can guess the key or recovery code.
A checksum is a short value computed from data and stored with it so that changes can be detected; a BIP 39 recovery code carries ENT/32 bits taken from a SHA-256 hash.
A keyed hash, or message authentication code, mixes a secret key into a hash so that only a holder of the key can produce or confirm the result; HMAC is the standard construction.
Key stretching derives a key from a secret by repeating a function many times, so that every guess of an attacker costs as much work as the honest computation.
The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it
A block is a group of transactions, marked with a time and committing to the previous block, that is added to the blockchain once it carries a valid proof of work.
The blockchain is the list of validated blocks, each linking to its predecessor all the way back to the first block; changing an old block breaks every later link.
A timestamp is a recorded time attached to data; each block carries one, and together they place the transactions in an agreed order.
A node is a computer that takes part in the Bitcoin network and runs software that speaks its protocol; full nodes validate blocks and may also route, mine or serve wallets.
The Computing section explains the ordinary technology on which Bitcoin software runs and by which people reach it
The Internet is a worldwide network of networks that uses the Internet protocol suite; Bitcoin users communicate over it primarily, although other transport networks can be used.
A protocol is a set of rules, formats and procedures that computers follow to exchange data; the Bitcoin protocol is the rules that nodes follow to talk to each other.
HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol, is the network protocol by which browsers and servers exchange web pages; its requests are plain text.
A web browser is a program that retrieves and displays pages from the web and lets users reach further pages through links.
A server is software or hardware that offers a service to clients over a network; Bitcoin's peer-to-peer design has no central server.
An API is a set of features and rules by which software interacts with other software; a third-party API client uses a remote system's API instead of the Bitcoin network.
A URI, a Uniform Resource Identifier, is a string that refers to a resource; the bitcoin: scheme of BIP 21 writes an address, an amount and a label as a URI.
A QR code is a two-dimensional matrix barcode that a camera can read; wallets use it to hand over addresses and payment requests without typing.
A database is a storage system that collects organized data so that it is easier to search, structure and extend; a wallet keeps its labels and history in one.
An operating system is system software that manages a computer's hardware and software resources and provides common services to programs; wallets run on top of one.
A distributed system is a set of computers that communicate over a network and work together; Bitcoin is a distributed system with no central server.
A bit is a binary digit, a byte is eight bits, and a hexadecimal digit stands for four bits; a 256-bit hash is 32 bytes or 64 hexadecimal digits.

The Threats section explains two attacks that chapter 1 warns about by name or by description: malicious software that steals or destroys, and phishing, which tricks a person into handing over a secret
Malware is software intentionally designed to cause harm, to leak information or to gain unauthorised access; fake wallet applications are the chapter's example.
Phishing is a scam in which attackers deceive people into revealing sensitive information or installing malware; a wallet that asks for the recovery code at an unexpected time is a warning sign.
The Nature branch answers a question that precedes all the others: what kind of thing is Bitcoin? Chapter 1 gives two complementary answers
The Characteristic section collects four properties that the chapter attributes to the bitcoin currency: it is virtual, it is borderless, it is decentralized, and it is robust
The bitcoin currency is entirely virtual: there are no physical coins or even individual digital coins, only transactions that imply the coins.
Bitcoin is fast, secure and borderless, which the chapter gives as the reason that it is arguably the perfect form of money for the internet.
Bitcoin is decentralized by design and free of any central authority or point of control that can be attacked or corrupted.
A robust digital currency is built to withstand intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements, which a decentralized design makes possible.
The Architecture section describes how the Bitcoin system is put together
The Bitcoin protocol defines a decentralized peer-to-peer network in which every full node is a peer that both provides and consumes services.
The second part of Bitcoin is a public transaction journal, the blockchain, in which every confirmed transaction is recorded for anyone to read.
The consensus rules are the set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance that every participant applies in the same way.
